title: Should You Buy Tesla Stock Before December?

Should You Buy Tesla Stock Before December?
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) has had a challenging year. Despite its core electric vehicle (EV) business often performing better than expected, partly due to soaring oil prices, the company's shares have significantly lagged broader equities. However, the year isn't over, and there is a chance Tesla could finish 2026 with a bang, given ongoing developments. With that said, should investors consider buying the stock before December?

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

A merger might be in the works

Tesla's CEO, Elon Musk, now leads two publicly traded corporations, the other being Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX), which went public in June. Rumors of a potential merger between Tesla and SpaceX have been circulating since before SpaceX was public, but a comment Musk made during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call added fuel to the fire.

Musk said that SpaceX and Tesla have formed independent special committees to discuss a potential merger between the two corporations. And more recently, five board directors from both companies have reportedly been discussing a potential all-stock merger that would make the combined entity worth about $3.5 trillion, with a deal possible by year-end. Importantly, this hasn't been confirmed by either company. But it's still worth figuring out the potential benefits and risks of this proposed acquisition.

Not necessarily a great deal

Suppose SpaceX acquires Tesla at a 20% premium in an all-stock deal: SpaceX would have to issue a substantial number of new shares, thereby significantly diluting existing shareholders. Tesla's stock might rise, at least initially, while SpaceX's could decline unless investors believe the merger will generate enough synergies to justify the acquisition premium.

There are indeed some reasons to think that the combined entity could create more value than either would on its own. For instance, both Tesla and SpaceX are investing massive sums in artificial intelligence (AI). As a single entity, they could eliminate redundant investments and lower costs, while leveraging their larger size to negotiate better deals with suppliers.

Also, some of Tesla's work, including its energy infrastructure and the Optimus humanoid robot, could be of immense value to SpaceX. So, that could be good news for the business' long-term prospects, although whether the proposed combined entity will, on balance, create more value is by no means guaranteed. However, one major source of uncertainty will likely come from regulators. The deal will probably attract significant attention from lawmakers, at least some of whom may try to stop it.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) shares slipped 1.18% to $380.14 at the 4:00 p.m. ET close on November 25, after the European Commission pushed a discussion on approving the company's supervised driving software back to December 15. The Technical Committee for Motor Vehicles had been expected to take up the system, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, on December 1, according to the Dutch regulator RDW.

The process has dragged since the RDW granted approval on April 10, with no vote at two earlier committee meetings. Twelve countries have recognized the Dutch approval, covering about 29% of the EU population, Electrek estimated in its report. EU-wide approval requires at least 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the population, and a rejection would invalidate national approvals already granted. No reason has been given for the delay. Elon Musk said on the third-quarter call that he would be surprised if approval took longer than the first quarter of 2027.

The math explains the stakes: Tesla needs to more than double its population coverage, from roughly 29% to 65%, and Germany alone would lift it to about 47%. Each delay could push European software revenue further out, while a rejection would reverse progress. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 87/100, with a strong balance sheet and good momentum but profitability that ranks below other mega-cap tech names. GF Value of $361.36 implies a 5.2% premium and a "fairly valued" label, so the price already assumes autonomy milestones land roughly on time. The next test is the December 15 committee meeting.

Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer XPeng (NYSE:XPEV) is preparing to enter the commercial humanoid robotics market with its Iron robot, targeting sales in the second quarter of 2027 at a price comparable to an electric vehicle.

The move opens another potential revenue stream for XPeng while positioning the Chinese automaker as an emerging competitor to Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA), which is also betting heavily on humanoid robots as a long-term growth opportunity.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with XPEV.

Is XPEV fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

XPEV GF Value chart

XPeng develops and sells smart electric vehicles, generating most of its revenue from vehicle deliveries. The company has also invested heavily in autonomous driving technology, software and robotics as it looks to diversify beyond the increasingly competitive Chinese EV market.

What makes XPeng's latest development particularly interesting is its commercial sales timeline. Moving humanoid robots beyond demonstrations and into customers' hands represents an important test of whether the technology can become a commercially viable business.

Pricing the robot near the cost of an electric vehicle could make it accessible to some commercial customers, although its practical capabilities and operating costs will ultimately determine demand.

XPeng plans to begin mass production of Iron's hardware in January 2027, with the robots initially training as retail assistants at the company's dealerships before becoming commercially available.

Vice Chairman Brian Gu told Bloomberg that XPeng aims to sell tens of thousands of robots in 2027.

Beyond hardware sales, XPeng plans to generate recurring revenue through software subscriptions and services for third-party developers.

The diversification push comes as XPeng continues navigating intense competition in China's EV market. Third-quarter vehicle revenue jumped 19.8% year over year to $3.23 billion, although the company remained unprofitable.

Investors Takeaway

XPeng's commercialization timeline raises the competitive stakes for Tesla's Optimus robotics business.

For XPeng investors, the January production milestone and second-quarter commercial launch will be important catalysts in 2027.

Investors should monitor manufacturing costs, initial customer orders, production volumes and software subscription revenue to determine whether robotics can eventually become a meaningful earnings contributor.

However, aggressive expansion could also increase research and development expenses, putting additional pressure on XPeng's profitability.

For Tesla investors, XPeng's pricing strategy introduces another competitive variable in a market widely viewed as a major source of future growth for the American automaker.

title: Elon Musk didn’t sell a single share in SpaceX’s record $85.7B IPO. Anthropic’s 7 cofounders cashed out $1.96B in theirs

Elon Musk didn’t sell a single share in SpaceX’s record $85.7B IPO. Anthropic’s 7 cofounders cashed out $1.96B in theirs

Trading disclosure

When Elon Musk took SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) public in June in what was then the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, he didn't sell a single share. Five months later, Anthropic's (NASDAQ: ANT) seven cofounders took a different approach, putting nearly $2 billion worth of their personal shares up for sale in an even bigger debut.

According to filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Anthropic's cofounders put more than 23.6 million of their own shares up for sale during the IPO. At the IPO price of $83, those shares were worth $1.96 billion before fees, with the proceeds going directly to the founders rather than the company.

Each cofounder was slated to sell nearly 3.4 million shares, worth $280.4 million. Separate SEC filings confirmed that CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic President and Board Chair Daniela Amodei, completed their sales on Nov. 20.

Despite the size of the payouts, the sales represent only about 1.4% of each founder's pre-IPO holdings. SpaceX, by contrast, raised money exclusively through the sale of newly issued shares. None of its existing shareholders, including Musk, received proceeds from the IPO.

While Anthropic's founders were able to sell at the IPO price, investors who bought shares on the open market experienced significant volatility. CNBC's Jim Cramer criticized the offering, arguing that too many shares had been allocated to institutional investors looking to make a quick profit. Anthropic's stock gained 17% in its Nasdaq debut before falling nearly 16% over the next three sessions, according to Yahoo Finance data.

As of Nov. 26, Anthropic shares were trading just below their $83 IPO price.

Why Musk isn't cashing out of SpaceX

Musk agreed to a 366-day lockup period that restricts him from selling his SpaceX shares until June 2027, subject to certain exceptions. Such agreements are common following IPOs and help prevent large shareholders from flooding the market with stock shortly after a company goes public.

Anthropic's founders agreed to similar restrictions, but unlike Musk, they had the opportunity to sell shares through the IPO itself. Meanwhile, Musk doesn't seem eager to cash out once those restrictions are lifted.

Key Takeaways

General Motors stock is up 11% in the past month, mostly on its move to Nasdaq, while the Nasdaq-100 fell 10%.

Ford's higher profit floor and a shift out of Tesla helped too, but Ford expects flat 2027 profit.

At 6.0x forward earnings with a $20 billion buyback, GM still looks like a buy ahead of its 2027 outlook in late January.

General Motors (GM:NASDAQ) stock is up 11% in the past month, while the Nasdaq-100 fell 10%. Most of the gain came from its move to Nasdaq, where it began trading on Nov. 17, in time to make the cutoff that Walmart missed last year for the Nasdaq-100's December reshuffle. If GM gets in, index funds that track the Nasdaq-100 would have to buy the stock.

Ford (F:NYSE) helped too, raising the floor of its profit outlook a day after GM's news. And investors moved money from Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) to Detroit after the Nov. 3 midterms.

Ford's raise came with a warning

On Oct. 28, Ford raised the low end of its 2026 adjusted EBIT guidance to $10.5 billion from $10 billion. But it expects 2027 profit to be about flat, and analysts have its normalized EPS at $1.89 for 2026 and $1.87 for 2027. GM faces the same squeeze: CFO Paul Jacobson put its 2027 commodity headwind at roughly $2 billion.

Tesla lost what Detroit gained. It trades at 180x forward earnings and fell after Nov. 3 on worries that a Democratic Congress could slow a possible merger with SpaceX. Money that moved on politics can move back just as fast.

Still about 6x earnings

Analysts expect GM's normalized net income to stay near $12 billion a year through 2028, so EPS growth comes from buybacks, including a new $20 billion authorization. Consensus has normalized EPS climbing from $10.60 in 2025 to $16.16 in 2028:

The $101 consensus target is about 6.3x GM's 2028 EPS estimate, so the stock only needs those estimates to hold to get there.

Key Takeaways

Tesla and SpaceX sank early on Nov. 25 before paring losses; SpaceX closed up 1.3% and Tesla down 1.2%.

JPMorgan said S&P could waive some entry rules after a merger, bringing passive buying of roughly 10% of SpaceX's free float.

Index funds could then keep the SpaceX shares they receive.

SpaceX may not need a waiver: by June 2027, its $4.3 billion first-quarter loss drops out of S&P's four-quarter profit test.

Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) and SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) shareholders had a volatile Wednesday. SpaceX stock fell more than 8% early on Nov. 25 and Tesla nearly 6%, as merger worries met a tech selloff, before SpaceX closed up 1.3% and Tesla down 1.2%.

The worry is the share swap. The Future Fund's Gary Black estimates SpaceX would have to issue 52% new shares to buy Tesla at a 25% premium, a premium he expects "will shrivel to zero as merger arbs short their anticipated SPCX proceeds." In a follow-up post, he pointed to Marvell Technology (MRVL:NASDAQ), down 43% over the past month on worries about its all-stock deal for Lumentum (LITE:NASDAQ).

JPMorgan sees a bright spot. In a Nov. 24 note, its analysts said past cases suggest S&P's index committee could waive some entry rules to let SpaceX into the S&P 500 after a Tesla deal, triggering passive buying of roughly 10% of its free-float shares.

Close on Profits, Short on Time

The S&P 500 requires 12 months of trading and positive GAAP net income in the latest quarter and over the last four combined. Having listed in June, SpaceX can't be considered until June 2027. It's closer on profits. Analysts expect its normalized EPS to rise from $0.28 this year to $2.91 in 2027 and $5.98 in 2028:

SPCX Normalized EPS Estimates: 2026-2028 (TIKR)

S&P's test uses GAAP net income, which SpaceX only just turned positive:

SPCX Quarterly Net Income: Last 6 Quarters (TIKR)

Its $4.4 billion third-quarter profit, including a $561 million Boring Company gain, didn't cover the $4.8 billion first-half loss. A fourth-quarter profit above about $0.4 billion would put 2026 in the black, and by June 2027, the $4.3 billion first-quarter loss drops out of the count.

Index Funds Already Own Tesla

Every S&P 500 index fund holds Tesla. If SpaceX buys Tesla in an all-stock deal, they'd get SpaceX shares, and if SpaceX weren't in the index, they'd have to sell them. With a waiver, they'd keep them and buy more. Tesla also gives S&P a reason to bend, with a GAAP profit in every one of the last eight quarters:

On November 25, 2026, SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) committed to contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account. The same release said CEO Elon Musk "will personally match the number of shares donated by SpaceX", so each active account would get two shares: one from the company and one from Musk.

SpaceX closed that day at $127.44, up 1.3%. At that close, two shares are worth about $254.88 per account.

The small gain did little to offset a steep fall. The stock fell 11.19% over the past week and 13.25% over the past month, and it is down 20.82% since June 12, 2026.

SPCX Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

SpaceX said ownership of the company "should extend to the next generation of Americans." The release left out the details shareholders need: how many accounts qualify, when the shares move, and where Musk's shares come from.

Committed Shares Versus Intended Shares

The release itself describes these as "intended future contributions of Class A common stock" and lists "third-party and government approvals" among the risks. It gives no account count, no total value, and no transfer date.

Musk's match is a personal pledge, and the release does not say whether he will use his own shares or new stock. He first posted in October that he would give a share to every child in America.
